title: Yasa's night
hookLine: a rich young man wakes after a party, sickened, and walks out into the night (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)

lines: A RICH YOUNG MAN NAMED YASA.
cards: Three in the morning. The party's over, but nobody went home. People asleep on the cushions, on the floor, one still clutching a lute.
The music stopped a while ago. One young man is awake, looking at it all, and something turns in his stomach that isn't the food.
His name is Yasa, son of a very rich family in Benares, with a house for every season and musicians who played for him through the night. Tonight he woke before everyone else.

teach.b: The old monastic rulebook, the Vinaya, tells it vividly. The lamps are still burning, and Yasa sees the musicians and attendants asleep around him, sprawled in every direction, mouths open, instruments dropped.

The text says it looked to him like a cemetery. He cries out: how distressing this is, how oppressive. He puts on his golden slippers and walks out of the house, out of the city gate, into the dark, toward the Deer Park.
And the Buddha, the story says, is walking up and down in the open air before dawn. He hears Yasa's cry and answers: this is not distressing, this is not oppressive.
Come, Yasa, sit down. I'll teach you. So a young man in party clothes and golden slippers sits on the ground with a wandering teacher, listens, and something in him settles.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA'S STORY IN ONE NIGHT.
teach.b: Some readers notice how much it sounds like another story.
A young man of a rich family, pleasure all around him, a night when he looks at sleeping bodies and sees the truth under the glitter, a walk out into the dark. That's the Buddha's own going forth.
Yasa lives it in one night, and this time someone is waiting on the road. And his name, Yasa, means fame, or glory.

The man named Fame found the party empty. It doesn't stop with him. His father comes searching, following the tracks of those golden slippers, and becomes the first lay follower to take the three refuges.
His mother and his former wife become the first women lay followers. And Yasa's friends come looking for him too. Tomorrow, where that leads.

how: Buddhists tell Yasa's story as one of the first conversions after the Deer Park, and remember his father as the first lay follower to take refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, as lay Buddhists still do today.

o: the night a rich young man walked out to the Buddha
a full-moon festival night of lamps and music
a farmer's prayer for rain after a dry season

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a name meaning fame, or glory
looked to him like a cemetery
the first lay follower to take refuge

s: Yasa was a poor boy looking for food
he was the son of a very rich family in Benares.
the Buddha answered Yasa's cry: come, sit down
this is not distressing, he said. come, Yasa, sit down. I'll teach you.
Yasa's mother and former wife became the first women lay followers
the family followed him, one by one.

games.q: you're Yasa. it's before dawn, the party is over, and the room suddenly looks like a cemetery. what do you do?
o: wake everyone up and start again.
put on your slippers and walk out into the night.
games.why: he walks out of the house and out of the city gate, toward the Deer Park, and finds the Buddha walking there before dawn.

practice: Think of something you keep doing that doesn't give you what it used to: an app you open without meaning to, a habit gone flat, a place you go because you always have. Picture it the way Yasa saw that room, with the lamps still on.
You don't have to hate it; just see it clearly, and imagine standing up and walking out the door.

wordCard.voice: Yasa's night. A rich young man wakes after a party, sees it clearly, walks out into the dark, and finds the Buddha on the road.

orig.note: Pali: fame, glory, renown. Sanskrit yaśas.

carryVoice: Your line: walk out of the party. Golden slippers, a dark road, and a teacher at the end of it. Until tomorrow.
